The accused has been put up for trial for the offence under sections 498-A/ 304-B/ 34 of IPC with the allegations that he had harassed his wife to meet unlawful demand of dowry which resulted into death of his wife.
BRIEF FACTS OF THE CASE 1.0
As per the prosecution story, on 01.06.2018, DD No. 57Awas received from HAH Centerry Hospital that wife of the accused namely Pooja Tanwar had committed suicide.
SI Satyavir reached the hospital and collected the MLC.
SI Satyavir along with HC Samman Khan got preserved the dead body and thereafter, inspection was conducted by Inspection Mobile Crime Team.
Postmortem report was handed over to SI Satyavir.
SI Satyavir Singh recorded the statement of brother of deceased in presence of Sh. Arvind Chopra, Tehsildar.

On the basis of allegations levelled by the brother of deceased and on the basis of initial enquiry, it was revealed that the accused had harassed his wife to meet unlawful demand of dowry which resulted into death of his wife.
FIR was registered and the matter was investigated.

After completion of the investigation,
the chargesheet was filed in the Court against the accused and his other family members for the State vs Sandeep Tanwar And Ors on 17 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/30892377/
1 offences u/s , 498-A, 304-B and 306 IPC.

Also, the other accused Rajkali was discharged from the present case.
Accused Sandeep Tanwar pleaded not guilty to the charge and claimed trial.
PROSECUTION EVIDENCE 3.0

The prosecution examined the following witnesses in support of its case :-

He deposed that on 16.05.2019 while being posted as Duty Officer at PS Tigri, he had registered the present FIR No. 137/2019 EX.PW1/A and issued the corresponding certificate under Section 65B Indian Evidence Act Ex.Pw1/C. 3.2 PW2

He deposed about the demands of dowry by the accused and consequent harassment and cruelty meted to his sister by the accused.
He also deposed about payments made by him pursuant to demands made by the accused.
I shall discuss his testimony in detail later.
This witness also deposed that the marriage card and photographs were handed over by him to the police vide seizure memo Ex.PW2/B.
He also identified the marriage ceremony photographs as Ex.P1 to P5.
He further deposed that his statement was recorded by the Executive Magistrate which he exhibited as Ex.PW2/A .
3.3 PW-3 is Rajpal.
He is the father of the deceased.
He deposed on similar lines as that of PW2.
This witness exhibited his statement before the Executive Magistrate as Ex.PW3/A .
He also identified his signatures on the dead body identification memo of deceased Ms. Pooja which was exhibited as Ex.PW3/B. 3.4 PW4 is Sukhram.
He deposed that he acted as the mediator for the marriage of the deceased Ms. Pooja to accused which was solemnized no 24.11.2017 in the presence of this witness.

3.8 No other witness was examined by the prosecution and Prosecution Evidence was closed.
STATEMENT OF ACCUSED 4.0
All the incriminating circumstances appearing in the evidence was explained to the accused when he was examined under Section 313 Cr.P.C.

The accused denied all the allegations and gave only formal answers saying that he does not know anything about the evidence led against him and stated that he is innocent and has been falsely implicated in this case.
DEFENCE EVIDENCE 4.1
Accused examined himself as DW1 in his defence.

The accused took a defence that on 15.05.2019, he had an altercation with the deceased as she was in a habit of borrowing money for her personal expense from her brother and also from the brother of accused which he did not like.
After their small altercation, he left the house and then went to the gym.
He came back after around 45 minutes and found that Pooja had locked the door of the room.
He called his neighbours and broke the door.
Then he saw that the deceased was hanging from the fan from the ceiling in our room.
He then took her to hospital in an auto where she was declared dead. .
He claimed ignorance about the manner of death of his wife.
The accused however, did not lead any evidence in support of his defence.
ARGUMENTS 5.0
It was argued by Ld. Addl. PP that there are clear allegations of dowry demand and harassment on account of dowry.

It was argued that the death of the victim had occurred under suspicious circumstances within two years of marriage and the onus was upon the accused husband to explain the circumstances under which the victim died.
It was further argued that the accused failed to discharge the onus and that all the allegations stand proved on record.

It was argued that asking for monetary help from brother in law and sister in law does not amount to dowry demand.

It was further argued that no evidence was brought on record by the prosecution to prove the payments of Rs. 50,000/- or Rs.
1,00,000/-.

It was further argued that admittedly there is no complaint to any authority prior to the incident regarding any harassment on account of dowry which shows that the allegations in this regard are afterthought.
It was further argued that no evidence was brought on record to prove that immediately before her death, the victim was subjected to any cruelty.
6.0 I have heard the arguments addressed by the Ld. Addl. PP as well as Ld. Defence Counsel.
I have also gone through the entire record.
APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE & REASONING 7.0
Section 498A IPC makes 'cruelty' against a married woman by her husband or his relatives a punishable offence.

In order to attract the penal provisions of section 498A IPC, following ingredients must be satisfied :
a) the woman must be married;
b) she must be subjected to cruelty or harassment ; and,
c) such cruelty or harassment must've been shown either by the husband or by any relative of the husband.
7.1 Section 304B IPC defines and provides punishment for the offence of 'dowry death'.

The ingredients necessary to constitute the offence of dowry death have been succinctly recapitulated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Rajinder Singh vs. State of Punjab, Cr.Apl. no. 2321/09 decided on 26.02.2015.

entities.text: Rajinder Singh vs. State of Punjab, Cr.Apl. no. 2321/09
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The same are reproduced herein under :
"9.(a) death of a woman must have been caused by any burns or bodily injury or her death must have occurred otherwise than under normal circumstances;
(b) such death must have occurred within seven years of marriage;(c) soon before her death, she must have been subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband; and (d) such cruelty or harassment must be in connection with the demand for dowry".
In the case of Parvati Devi vs. The State of Bihar now Jharkhand and Ors. Crl. Apl. No. 574/2012 decided on 17.12.2021

entities.label: PRECEDENT

"The explanation appended to section 304B IPC states that the word 'dowry' shall have the same meaning as provided in section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 which reads as follows:

"2. Definition of dowry - In this act, "dowry"
means any property or valuable security given or agreed to be given either directly or indirectly- (a) by one party to a marriage to the other party to the marriage; or (b) by the parents of either party to the marriage by any other person, to either party to the marriage or to any other person;
at or before or any time after the marriage in connection with the marriage of the said parties, but does not include dower or mehr in the case of persons to whom the muslim personal law (shariat)
applies."

7.2 Coming next to section 113B of the Evidence Act, the same refers to a presumption relating to 'dowry death' and is phrased below :
"113B. Presumption as to dowry death.-

When the question is whether a person has committed the dowry death of a woman and it is shown that soon before her death such woman had been subjected to cruelty or harassment for, or in connection with,
any demand for dowry, the court shall presume that such person had caused the dowry death.
Explanation.
For the purposes of this section, dowry death shall have the same meaning as in section 304B of the Indian Penal Code(45 of 1860)."

7.3 Section 304B IPC read in conjunction with section 113B of the evidence act leaves no manner of doubt that once the prosecution has been able to demonstrate that a woman has been subjected to cruelty or harassment for or in connection with any demand for dowry, soon before her death, the court shall proceed on a presumption that the persons who have subjected her to cruelty or harassment in connection with the demand for dowry, have caused a dowry death within the meaning of section 304B IPC.

The said presumption is, however, rebuttable and can be dispelled on the accused being able to demonstrate through cogent evidence that all the ingredients of section 304B IPC have not been satisfied.
Reference in this regard may be had to Parvati Devi's case (supra).
8.0 Coming to the facts of the instant case, it is not in dispute that the victim had suffered an unnatural death.
She was found hanging at her matrimonial house on 15.05.2019 and was taken to the hospital where she was declared brought dead.
As per the post-mortem report Ex.PX2, ligature marks were seen on the neck in addition to contusion on the left arm.
The cause of death was opined to be asphyxia due to ante-mortem hanging.

8.1 PW2 Vedpal, who is the brother of the deceased and also the complainant of the present case,
deposed unequivocally about the cruelty and harassment suffered by her deceased sister at the hands of the accused.

He categorically deposed that even though sufficient stridhan had been given to deceased sister at the time of her marriage, a few months after the marriage, the accused started State vs Sandeep Tanwar And Ors on 17 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/30892377/
5 taunting her for not bringing enough dowry.

entities.text: State vs Sandeep Tanwar And Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: He narrated in detail the ordeal his deceased sister had to go through at her matrimonial home.
He deposed that few months after the wedding, the accused demanded Rs.50,000/- from him on the ground that his brother Amardeep and Amardeep's wife had a dire need of money.
He also deposed that he had himself paid Rs.50,000/- to the accused.
He further deposed that a few moths thereafter, accused alongwith the deceased visited his house and demanded Rs. 1,00,000/-.
As PW2 could not fulfill the demand at that time, the accused left the deceased at PW2's house and did not take her back till the time the amount was not paid.
8.2 During his cross-examination, PW2 stated that both the sums of money Rs.50,000/- and Rs.1,00,000/- were paid by him in cash to accused Sandeep at his residence.
He categorically stated that he had to give in to the demands as his sister told him that accused Sandeep wanted money as sufficient dowry was not given.

He further deposed that in the month of saavan in the year 2018, he had visited the matrimonial house of his sister with gifts, however, the inlaws of his sister demanded a Wagon-R car failing which they threatened to destroy the life of his sister.
He could not fulfill the demand and again in the month of January/February 2019, accused Sandeep demanded Rs 20 lacs on the ground that his brother Amardeep had to purchase a flat in Dwarka.
He again expressed his inability to fulfill the demand.
His sister told him that if he could not fulfill the demand, her inlaws would harass and torture her.
She even told him that either they would kill her or she would be compelled to commit suicide.
During cross-examination, PW2 further stated that 10-15 days prior to 28.04.2019, the accused had again left the deceased at PW2's house as he could not fulfill the demand of Rs.20 lacs.
On 28.04.2019, the deceased told PW2 that in case he could not fulfill the demand, the inlaws would kill her or she will commit suicide.
Thereafter, after much persuasion and assurances given by PW2 to make arrangements for payment, the accused agreed to take back the deceased.
He also deposed that on the day of her death, the deceased had called PW2 on his mobile phone and told him that the accused demanded Rs.15,000/- on the ground that the money was needed for Amardeep.
When she refused, the accused started to snatch her chain.
PW2 remained firm on his deposition during sustained cross-examination.
He denied the suggestions of the Ld. Defence Counsel and his credit could not be shaken despite lengthy cross-examination.
Further, as deposed by PW2, the demands were made from him and the payments of Rs.50,000/- and Rs.1,00,000/- were also deposed to have been made by him.

Further,
on more than one occasion, the accused left the deceased at the house of PW2 and refused to take her back until his demands were fulfilled.
The deposition in this regard also is not hearsay as the PW2 was privy to the same.
Hence, it cannot be said that the version of PW2 is based on hearsay facts as sought to be argued by Ld. Counsel for the accused.
His testimony was also corroborated by PW3, the father of deceased.
8.3 PW3 Rajpal Yadav also deposed about the demands of dowry from accused side and the harassment suffered by his deceased daughter.
He corroborated the allegations of demand of Rs.50,000/- and Rs.1,00,000/- by the accused and payments of said amounts by his son PW2.
He further corroborated the allegation of demand of Wagon-R car and Rs.20 lacs by the accused.

He deposed that his family could not fulfill said demands and due to this reason his daughter was State vs Sandeep Tanwar And Ors on 17 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/30892377/
6 tortured by her inlaws.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: He also remained firm during the cross-examination and nothing damning to the case of the prosecution could be elicited.

8.4 It was argued by Ld. defence Counsel that seeking financial assistance for brother or sister in law of the husband for purchasing a flat would not amount to dowry demand and that it was the deceased who herself asked for money from her brother and also from the brother of the accused.
This argument of Ld. defence Counsel cannot be accepted.

In Rajinder Singh's case (supra), it was observed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that any money or property or valuable security demanded by any of the persons mentioned in Section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, at or before or at anytime after the marriage which is reasonably connected to the death of a married woman, would necessarily be in connection with or in relation to the marriage unless, the facts of a given case clearly and unequivocally point otherwise.
8.5

Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, in the case of State of M.P. vs. Jogendra & Anr.
Crl. (Apl.) no. 190/2012 decided on 11.01.2022, held as under :
" 14. ...

State of M.P. vs. Jogendra & Anr.
Crl. (Apl.) no. 190/2012
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: We are of the opinion that the trial court has correctly interpreted the demand for money raised by the respondents on the deceased for construction of a house as falling within the definition of the word 'dowry'.

The submission made by learned Counsel for the respondents that the deceased was also a party to such a demand as she had on her own asked her mother and maternal uncle to contribute to the construction of the house, must be understood In the correct perspective.

It cannot be lost sight of that the respondents had been tormenting the deceased and asking her to approach her family members for money to build a house and it was only on their persistence and insistence that she was compelled to ask them to contribute some amount for constructing a house."
8.6 Hence, demand of money for purchasing a flat for brother of husband would be considered as dowry demand, in my view.

9.0 It was further argued that admittedly, no complaint regarding any dowry related harassment was lodged by deceased or her family members prior to the incident in question, which shows that the allegations are not true and an afterthought.

In the case of Preetpal Singh vs. The State of UP &
Anr., Crl. Apl. No.520/2020 decided on 14.08.2020, the Hon'ble Supreme Court opined that failure to lodge an FIR complaining of dowry and harassment before the death of the victim is inconsequential as the parents and family members of the victim obviously would not want to precipitate a complete breakdown of marriage by lodging an FIR.

entities.text:
Preetpal Singh vs. The State of UP &
Anr
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Hence, the argument in this regard of Ld. defence Counsel is rejected.

10.0 It was vociferously argued by the Ld. defence Counsel that there is no evidence on record to suggest that soon before her death, the deceased was subjected to harassment related to dowry demand and hence, section 304B IPC would not be attracted.

Before answering the same, it would be apposite to quote from the decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sher Singh vs. State of Haryana,
2015 (1) SCALE 250) .

entities.text:
Sher Singh vs. State of Haryana,
2015 (1) SCALE 250)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It was held as under :
State vs Sandeep Tanwar And Ors on 17 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/30892377/
7

entities.text: State vs Sandeep Tanwar And Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
"We are aware that the word 'soon' finds place in section 304B; but we would prefer to interpret its use not in the terms of days or months or years, but as necessarily indicating that the demand of dowry should not be stale or an aberration of the past,
but should be the continuing cause for the death under section 304B or the suicide under section 306 of the IPC.

Once the presence of these concomitants are established or shown or proved by the prosecution, even by preponderance of possibility, the initial presumption of innocence is replaced by an assumption of guilt of the accused, thereupon transferring the heavy burden of proof upon him and requiring him to produce evidence dislodging his guilt, beyond reasonable doubt."

The above view was endorsed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rajinder Singh's case (supra) by holding as under :
"23. We endorse what has been said by these two decisions.
Days or months are not what is to be seen.
What must be borne in mind is that the word 'soon' does not mean ' immediate'.
A fair and pragmatic construction keeping in mind the great social evil that has led to the enactment of section 304B would make it clear that the expression is a relative expression.
Time lags may differ from case to case.
All that is necessary is that the demand for dowry should not be stale but should be the continuing cause for death of the married woman."
11.0 Coming back to the facts of the case in hand, the death of deceased occurred on 15.05.2019.
As per the testimony of PW2, 10-15 days prior to 28.04.2019, the accused had left the deceased at PW2's house and refused to take her back until the demand of Rs.20 lacs was fulfilled.
On 28.04.2019, after much persuasion, the accused agreed to take the deceased back when PW2 assured to make arrangement of money soon.
This shows that the harassment was continuing till that time.

Further, it has come in the evidence of PW2 that on the date of her death, the deceased had called him on his mobile phone informing about demand of Rs.15,000/- and attempts to snatch her chain by the accused on her refusal to accede to such demand.
On the very same day, she died an unnatural death.
This shows that the demand of dowry did not cease and was continuing even on the day of death of the victim.
Hence, it is pellucid that soon before her death, the victim was subjected to cruelty and harassment in connection with demand of dowry.
12.0 As noted above, the testimonies of PW2 and PW3 are found to be reliable and consistent despite a thorough cross- examination.
Both the witnesses appear trustworthy and their testimony inspires confidence.

Taking into account the evidence on record, particularly the testimony of brother of deceased, I am of the opinion that necessary ingredients of section 498A and 304B IPC are made out against the accused.

12.1 Once the necessary ingredients under section 304B IPC stands satisfied, a presumption of causation arises against the accused under section 113B of the Evidence Act that it was the accused who had caused the dowry death of the victim.
The onus falls upon the accused to rebut the statutory presumption.

The accused while deposing as DW1 denied making any dowry demand and claimed that it was the deceased who was in the habit of borrowing money from her brother as well State vs Sandeep Tanwar And Ors on 17 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/30892377/
8 as the brother of accused as she wanted a lavish lifestyle.

entities.text: State vs Sandeep Tanwar And Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: But no evidence to support such a claim was produced.
Further, during cross- examination, the accused gave evasive replies and feigned ignorance as to whether he had demanded Rs.51,000/- at the time of vidaai ceremony.

Also, as noted above, the testimonies of PW2 and PW3 regarding dowry demands made by the accused inspire confidence and appear completely trustworthy and the defence could not shake the credit of the prosecution witnesses despite thorough and lengthy cross-examination.
The accused also claimed that on the day of the incident, he had an argument with the deceased and thereafter, he went to a gym near his house.
When he returned, the door was bolted from inside.
He broke open the door with the help of neigbours and found the deceased hanging.
Again, it is mere bald averment.
No cogent evidence was led in support of the same.
Neither anyone from the gym nor any such neighbour was called to testify.
In the absence of any convincing piece of evidence, the same does not lend any credence to the defence of the accused.
I am of the opinion that the accused failed to discharge the onus to rebut the presumption under section 113B of the evidence act.
13.0 The prosecution has been successful in establishing a water tight case against the accused.
From the evidence brought on record, it stands proved that the accused being the husband of the victim had treated her with cruelty and harassed her in connection with demands of dowry.

Further,
the victim died an unnatural death under mysterious circumstances in her matrimonial house within two years of her marriage.
Also, it stands proved on record that soon before her death, the victim was subjected to cruelty and harassment in relation to dowry demands at the hands of the accused.
All the ingredients of section 498A as well as 304B IPC are squarely made out.
13.1 Accordingly, accused Sandeep Tanwar is convicted for the offences punishable under sections 498A and 304B IPC.

(b) such death must have occurred within seven years of marriage;(c) soon before her death, she must have been subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband; and (d) such cruelty or harassment must be in connection with the demand for dowry".

7.3 Section 304B IPC read in conjunction with section 113B of the evidence act leaves no manner of doubt that once the prosecution has been able to demonstrate that a woman has been subjected to cruelty or harassment for or in connection with any demand for dowry, soon before her death, the court shall proceed on a presumption that the persons who have subjected her to cruelty or harassment in connection with the demand for dowry, have caused a dowry death within the meaning of section 304B IPC.
The said presumption is, however, rebuttable and can be dispelled on the accused being able to demonstrate through cogent evidence that all the ingredients of section 304B IPC have not been satisfied.

11.0 Coming back to the facts of the case in hand, the death of deceased occurred on 15.05.2019.
As per the testimony of PW2, 10-15 days prior to 28.04.2019, the accused had left the deceased at PW2's house and refused to take her back until the demand of Rs.20 lacs was fulfilled.
On 28.04.2019, after much persuasion, the accused agreed to take the deceased back when PW2 assured to make arrangement of money soon.
Further, it has come in the evidence of PW2 that on the date of her death, the deceased had called him on his mobile phone informing about demand of Rs.15,000/- and attempts to snatch her chain by the accused on her refusal to accede to such demand.
On the very same day, she died an unnatural death.
This shows that the demand of dowry did not cease and was continuing even on the day of death of the victim.
Hence, it is pellucid that soon before her death, the victim was subjected to cruelty and harassment in connection with demand of dowry.
12.0 As noted above, the testimonies of PW2 and PW3 are found to be reliable and consistent despite a thorough cross- examination.
Both the witnesses appear trustworthy and their testimony inspires confidence.
Taking into account the evidence on record, particularly the testimony of brother of deceased, I am of the opinion that necessary ingredients of section 498A and 304B IPC are made out against the accused.
12.1 Once the necessary ingredients under section 304B IPC stands satisfied, a presumption of causation arises against the accused under section 113B of the Evidence Act that it was the accused who had caused the dowry death of the victim.
The onus falls upon the accused to rebut the statutory presumption.
No cogent evidence was led in support of the same.
Neither anyone from the gym nor any such neighbour was called to testify.
In the absence of any convincing piece of evidence, the same does not lend any credence to the defence of the accused.
I am of the opinion that the accused failed to discharge the onus to rebut the presumption under section 113B of the evidence act.
13.0 The prosecution has been successful in establishing a water tight case against the accused.
From the evidence brought on record, it stands proved that the accused being the husband of the victim had treated her with cruelty and harassed her in connection with demands of dowry.
Further,
the victim died an unnatural death under mysterious circumstances in her matrimonial house within two years of her marriage.
Also, it stands proved on record that soon before her death, the victim was subjected to cruelty and harassment in relation to dowry demands at the hands of the accused.
All the ingredients of section 498A as well as 304B IPC are squarely made out.
